items.followUp: Why is the path of light visible when it passes through a colloid?

rubric.why: The Tyndall effect is caused by light scattering from colloidal particles.
rubric.description: States that colloidal particles scatter light.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying light scattering by colloidal particles.

rubric.why: The scattered light makes the beam's path visible.
rubric.description: Links the scattering to the visible path of the light beam.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that scattering makes the path visible.

modelAnswer: Colloidal particles scatter the light passing through a colloid.
The scattered light makes the path of the beam visible; this is called the Tyndall effect.

items.followUp: Define a weak electrolyte and give one example.

rubric.why: A strong electrolyte ionizes or dissociates almost completely in aqueous solution or in the molten state.
rubric.description: Defines a strong electrolyte by its near-complete ionization or dissociation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it ionizes or dissociates almost completely.

rubric.why: An appropriate example demonstrates a strong electrolyte; strong electrolytes conduct electricity well.
rubric.description: Gives a suitable example of a strong electrolyte.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for an example such as sodium chloride (NaCl) or hydrochloric acid (HCl).

modelAnswer: A strong electrolyte is a substance that ionizes almost completely in aqueous solution or in the molten state.
It conducts electricity well; for example, sodium chloride (NaCl) is a strong electrolyte.

items.followUp: Write the chemical formula of magnesium chloride by using the valencies of its ions.

rubric.why: The formula-writing method begins by identifying the constituent elements or ions and their symbols.
rubric.description: Writes the symbols of the constituents for the worked example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly identifying calcium and chlorine as Ca and Cl.

rubric.why: The valencies determine the subscripts in the formula.
rubric.description: States the valencies of calcium and chlorine in the example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for Ca = 2 and Cl = 1.

rubric.why: Interchanging the valencies gives the initial subscripts.
rubric.description: Explains the interchange of valencies to form subscripts.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the interchange or criss-cross step.

rubric.why: Subscripts are reduced to the simplest whole-number ratio, and a subscript of 1 is omitted.
rubric.description: States how to simplify the subscripts and handle a subscript of 1.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for either reduction to the simplest ratio or omission of subscript 1.

rubric.why: The completed example has the correct formula CaCl₂.
rubric.description: Gives the correct final formula for calcium chloride.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for CaCl₂.

modelAnswer: Write the symbols of the elements or ions in the compound: Ca and Cl.
Write their valencies: Ca = 2 and Cl = 1.
Interchange the valencies and write them as subscripts: Ca₁Cl₂.
Reduce the subscripts to the simplest whole-number ratio, if possible.
Omit the subscript 1; therefore, the formula of calcium chloride is CaCl₂.

items.followUp: Define an ionic bond and describe how it forms in sodium chloride.

rubric.why: A covalent bond forms through the sharing of electron pairs between atoms.
rubric.description: Defines a covalent bond in terms of shared electron pairs.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the sharing-of-electrons definition.

rubric.why: One shared pair forms a single covalent bond.
rubric.description: Identifies a single covalent bond as one shared pair of electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the single-bond type and its shared-pair count.

rubric.why: Two shared pairs form a double covalent bond.
rubric.description: Identifies a double covalent bond as two shared pairs of electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the double-bond type and its shared-pair count.

rubric.why: Three shared pairs form a triple covalent bond.
rubric.description: Identifies a triple covalent bond as three shared pairs of electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the triple-bond type and its shared-pair count.

modelAnswer: A covalent bond is formed when atoms share one or more pairs of electrons.
A single covalent bond involves one shared pair, for example, in H₂.
A double covalent bond involves two shared pairs, for example, in O₂.
A triple covalent bond involves three shared pairs, for example, in N₂.

items.followUp: What are anode rays? Write four properties of anode rays.

rubric.why: Cathode rays are streams of electrons emitted from the cathode in a discharge tube.
rubric.description: Defines cathode rays as electrons or negatively charged particles emitted from the cathode.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the rays as electrons or negatively charged particles from the cathode.

rubric.why: Cathode rays propagate in straight lines.
rubric.description: States that cathode rays travel in straight lines.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this property.

rubric.why: Cathode rays are negatively charged and are deflected by electric or magnetic fields.
rubric.description: Gives a correct deflection property of cathode rays.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that they are deflected by a field or toward the positive plate.

rubric.why: Cathode rays cause certain substances to fluoresce when struck by them.
rubric.description: States that cathode rays produce fluorescence.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this property.

rubric.why: Cathode rays have mass and kinetic energy and can produce a heating effect on impact.
rubric.description: Gives a further valid property, such as mass, kinetic energy, or a heating effect.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one of these properties.

modelAnswer: Cathode rays are streams of electrons emitted from the cathode in a discharge tube.
They travel in straight lines.
They are deflected by electric and magnetic fields, showing that they are negatively charged.
They produce fluorescence when they strike certain substances.
They possess mass and kinetic energy and can produce a heating effect.

items.followUp: Define melting point and state the melting and boiling points of water at standard atmospheric pressure.

rubric.why: The freezing point is the temperature at which a liquid changes into a solid.
rubric.description: Defines freezing point using the correct phase change.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a liquid changes into a solid at its freezing point.

rubric.why: The boiling point is the temperature at which a liquid changes into a gas.
rubric.description: Defines boiling point using the correct phase change.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a liquid changes into a gas at its boiling point.

rubric.why: Water freezes at 0 °C at standard atmospheric pressure.
rubric.description: Gives the freezing point of water.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for 0 °C.

rubric.why: Water boils at 100 °C at standard atmospheric pressure.
rubric.description: Gives the boiling point of water.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for 100 °C.

modelAnswer: The freezing point is the temperature at which a liquid changes into a solid.
The boiling point is the temperature at which a liquid changes into a gas.
For water at standard atmospheric pressure, the freezing point is 0 °C.
At the same pressure, the boiling point of water is 100 °C.
